newsitem.title: USA: FULL TEXT - Texas Instrument Q4 loss.
newsitem.headline: FULL TEXT - Texas Instrument Q4 loss.

text.p: Texas Instruments Inc Thursday reported a fourth quarter loss of $29 million, or $0.15 a share vs a profit of $291 million, or $1.50 a share. The 1996 results include discontinued operations, and several one-time charges and asset write-downs.
This is the full text of the company's announcement. -----------PRESS RELEASE----------------------------

DALLAS, Jan. 23 /PRNewswire/ -- Texas Instruments Incorporated (NYSE: TXN) today announced its fourth quarter and year-end 1996 financial results in an environment of improving semiconductor market conditions and major actions to accelerate the pace of TI's strategic direction toward value, growth, and improved financial stability.

TI's earnings per share (EPS) in the fourth quarter of 1996 were $0.67, including catch-up royalties from the Samsung cross-licensing agreement and before the effect of special charges. Semiconductor performance in the fourth quarter of 1996 was up strongly from the third quarter, offsetting increased losses in mobile computing.

TI also announced today a definitive agreement for the sale of its mobile computing business to The Acer Group, based in Taipei, Taiwan. The sale is subject to certain government approvals and is expected to close on or before March 31, 1997. Financial terms were not disclosed.

The agreement includes the purchase by Acer of TI's award-winning TravelMate and Extensa product lines, and the associated assets of the business. It is expected that a substantial number of the worldwide employees dedicated to the mobile computing business will transfer to Acer upon closing. The agreement does not include the assets or people associated with TI's calculator business.

Note: As previously announced, TI and Raytheon Company have reached a definitive agreement under which Raytheon will purchase the assets of TI's defense business. As a result, 1996 and 1995 figures throughout this report have been adjusted to reflect defense as a discontinued business.
Financial Summary

TI's net revenues from continuing operations in 1996 were $9.9 billion, down from $11.4 billion in 1995, with most of the decrease due to a precipitous drop in dynamic random access memory (DRAM) prices. From the fourth quarter of 1995 to the fourth quarter of 1996, DRAM prices dropped about 80 percent. PFO from continuing operations in 1996, excluding special charges for cost-reduction actions and in-process R&D, was $374 million, down from $1439 million in 1995.

Net income for the year from continuing operations, excluding the special charges, was $281 million, compared with $996 million in 1995. Earnings per share from continuing operations, excluding the special charges, were $1.46, compared with $5.15 in 1995.

The special charges for continuing operations during 1996 included $192 million for in-process R&D associated with the purchase of Silicon Systems Inc. (SSi) in the third quarter, and $91 million in the fourth quarter for severance costs related to voluntary retirement and involuntary actions, as well as $117 million for asset write-downs on certain product lines, principally mobile computing.
Including the effect of the special charges, for TI's continuing operations, loss from operations for the year was $26 million; net loss was $46 million; and loss per share was $0.24.

Net revenues from continuing operations for the fourth quarter of 1996 were $2459 million, down 22 percent from $3147 million in the fourth quarter of 1995. Most of the decrease was due to sharply lower DRAM prices. Excluding the special charges, PFO from continuing operations in the fourth quarter was $173 million, net income was $95 million, and EPS were $0.50. This includes the impact of sharply lower mobile computing revenues, compared with the third quarter of 1996, which negatively impacted fourth quarter EPS by about $0.08 per share from the running rate of the prior quarter.

Results for the quarter also include $105 million in catch-up royalties for the first nine months of 1996 from the previously announced cross- licensing agreement with Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd., of Korea.

For TI's continuing operations, including the effect of these special charges and catch-up royalties, fourth quarter operating loss was $35 million; net loss was $40 million; and loss per share was $0.21.

Net income including discontinued operations for the year was $63 million, and in the fourth quarter of 1996, a net loss of $29 million. EPS including discontinued operations for the year 1996 were $0.33, and a loss per share of $0.15 for the fourth quarter.
Semiconductor

TI's semiconductor orders, while still below year-ago levels because of sharply lower DRAM prices, were up solidly from the third quarter of 1996. Orders for Digital Signal Processing Solutions (DSPS), comprised of digital signal processors plus mixed signal/analog products, grew more than 30 percent over the fourth quarter of 1995, with particular strength in wireless communications and mass storage applications.
TI's semiconductor revenues were also up sequentially from the prior quarter, although down from year-ago levels because of the severe decline in DRAM prices.

Revenues for DSPS continued to establish records and exceeded 40 percent of the company's total semiconductor revenues during the quarter. Differentiated product revenues were nearly two-thirds of the total.

Excluding charges, semiconductor operating profit was up significantly from the third quarter of 1996, as all product groups showed improvement. Memory, while improved, operated at a loss again due to continued lower prices and the high level of fixed investment.
Materials & Controls

Revenues in TI's materials and controls business were up moderately from the year-ago period. Profit from operations, excluding the charges, was up substantially, due primarily to cost efficiencies and improved productivity.
Personal Productivity Products

Revenues in TI's mobile computing business were down slightly from the year-ago level, and down sharply from the third quarter of 1996. Continued price pressures and lower than expected orders caused a greater loss over the year-ago and prior quarter periods. As expected, calculators operated at break-even in the fourth quarter after achieving substantial seasonal profits in the second and third quarters.
Emerging Opportunities

TI's digital imaging products continue to make steady progress in the transition from R&D to initial production, targeted at the very competitive commercial projection display market. The industry has recognized digital light processing (DLP) with the PC Magazine Technology of the Year Award. Two of TI's OEM customers also were recognized at the recent Consumer Electronics Show for their DLP-based consumer products.

The major long-term challenge continues to be cost reduction to levels that will permit participation in several markets. The company remains positive about the opportunity to build a high-growth business and expects to continue significant investments in 1997.

During the quarter, Texas Instruments Software released the commercial version of Performer, its department-level development tool. In October, Microsoft and Texas Instruments unveiled their joint repository design and a component information model, a key element of the repository. However, the market for TI's historical application development tools continues to weaken. The business is focusing on the rapidly emerging market for component-based development tools to achieve acceptable profit levels in the future.
Summary

TI's plans for 1997 are based on a moderate recovery in the world semiconductor market, with sustainable growth in electronic end equipment. Customer inventories of semiconductors are at historically low levels. DRAM prices remain volatile and the near-term memory market environment is expected to be difficult, although the bit growth rate remains strong. For continuing operations, capital expenditures in 1997 will be well below 1996, at about $1.1 billion, down from $2.1 billion. Excluding the one-time charge associated with the SSi acquisition, R&D will be increased to about $1.1 billion, up from $1.0 billion, primarily to support digital signal processing solutions and other advanced semiconductor technology.

"As we go forward, TI is intent on being a premier electronics company with a vision to achieve world leadership in digital solutions for the networked society -- a society transformed by personalized electronics, all speaking the same digital language, all able to communicate anytime, anywhere," said Tom Engibous, president and chief executive officer.

"We are accelerating our strategic direction by focusing on businesses, products and technologies that add value for TI and our customers through sustainable differentiation, with high growth opportunities, and improved financial stability.
"While we are making progress in implementing our strategy, we still have work to do, and 1997 will be a year of transition." (tabular material sent separately, headlined "full results")
